blocks.text: HarborWorks has two teaching requirements: accept as many nonoverlapping maintenance intervals as possible on one resource, and connect a set of sites using minimum total link weight. They sound similar because both ask for an optimum, yet their proofs use different structures. The first uses an exchange argument over finishing times. The second uses the cut property of spanning trees and a disjoint-set representation of connectivity.

blocks.text: A local decision is defined relative to the current partial solution. For interval scheduling, the candidate with the earliest finishing time leaves as much of the remaining time axis available as possible. For Kruskal’s spanning-tree algorithm, the next eligible edge has the smallest weight among the edges not yet considered and joins two currently separate components.

The algorithm did not suddenly become unreliable; the requested problem changed.

topics.title: 18.1.2 Recognizing Greedy-Solvable Problems
topics.summary: A useful proof pattern is exchange: take an optimal solution and show how to replace one of its choices with the greedy choice without making the objective worse or destroying feasibility. Then solve the smaller remaining problem using the same argument.

blocks.text: A useful proof pattern is exchange: take an optimal solution and show how to replace one of its choices with the greedy choice without making the objective worse or destroying feasibility. Then solve the smaller remaining problem using the same argument.
rich: A useful proof pattern is exchange: take an optimal solution and show how to replace one of its choices with the greedy choice without making the objective worse or destroying feasibility. Then solve the smaller remaining problem using the same argument.

blocks.text: For maximum-cardinality interval scheduling, choosing the compatible interval that finishes first leaves at least as much future time as any other first interval. Replace the first interval in an optimal schedule with that earliest-finishing one. Every later interval that followed the old first interval can still follow the replacement, so cardinality does not decrease.

blocks.text: The objective is essential. If jobs have different profits and the goal is maximum total profit, earliest finish need not be optimal. If jobs require setup gaps or multiple resources, feasibility changes. A proof belongs to its exact objective and constraints, not to the visual shape of the input table.

blocks.text: An exchange argument starts with an optimal solution and shows that its first decision can be replaced by the greedy choice without making the solution worse. Let the greedy interval finish no later than the first interval in an optimal schedule. Replacing that first interval with the greedy one cannot overlap a later interval that was compatible with the old first interval, because the replacement ends no later. The number of accepted intervals remains unchanged.

blocks.text: After making that replacement, the remaining problem has the same form: select the maximum number of intervals beginning at or after the chosen finish. Repeating the argument supports the full algorithm. The proof does not depend on a particular input order because the algorithm first orders candidates by finishing time.

blocks.text: Notice what the argument does not say. It does not say that the greedy choice appears in every optimum, nor that the optimal schedule is unique. Equal finishing times can admit several equally good choices. The companion breaks ties by start time to make its selection procedure explicit, but the cardinality proof is about feasibility and count, not about a unique identity sequence.

blocks.text: Use counterexample search as a practical companion to proof. Enumerate small interval sets, compare the greedy count with exhaustive subset selection, and inspect any disagreement. Exhaustive testing over a bounded universe does not prove the general theorem, but it can quickly reveal that a proposed rule such as “shortest duration first” or “earliest start first” lacks the required property. Treat a counterexample as a refinement of the specification and reasoning, not merely an inconvenient test.

A result containing three overlapping intervals is not redeemed by matching the expected count three. A result with a valid but smaller count exposes a different failure. When identity matters, retain stable record identifiers through sorting so the report can refer to the original requests rather than only to their positions in a reordered vector.
